catalog_quote: It goes without saying that we have no prior knowledge of Eblaite word stress. Nevertheless, one assumption can almost be taken for granted, namely that nominal case endings were unstressed. ... I therefore advance the hypothesis that, in source B of VE, the single phoneme /r/ was spelled r when followed by a stressed vowel but l when followed by an unstressed vowel. ... This suggests that Eblaite G-stem infinitives were stressed on the penult: /CaCáCum/, which is certainly in agreement with most Assyriologists’ expectations. ... The insight of the preceding paragraph can be extended to the more general rule that nouns are stressed on the penult when their penult is long (= contains a long vowel or is a closed syllable). ... [p.143] Spelling usage in source B of VE suggests that Eblaite word stress most frequently fell on the penult syllable, that is the last stem syllable, of nouns, especially when the penult was long. The existing data are insufficient for drawing conclusions on stress in other word classes such as finite verbal forms.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Reconstructed from orthography (l/r spelling of /r/ in one manuscript of the Vocabolario di Ebla): in nouns cited with a monosyllabic case ending (-um etc., assumed unstressed), stress fell on the penult = last stem syllable -- disyllables CV́C-um, G infinitives CaCáCum, long-penult nouns and also CVCCV́Cum with a short penult; evidence is firmest when the penult is heavy. Possible deviations: G participle CāCiCum perhaps antepenult (CáCiCum), ramānum perhaps initial. Nothing can be said about verbs or other word classes.
new_statements.exceptions: G-stem participle (CāCiCum) tentatively antepenult-stressed on 'admittedly sparse evidence' (p.140); ra-ma-nu-um 'self' would have first-syllable stress if the rule holds (p.140); geminate /rr/ always written r so uninformative; other Eblaite sources follow different spelling conventions, so the inference rests on source B of VE only.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress of nouns in citation form (stem + case ending) as glossed in a lexical list; explicitly a hypothesis for an extinct cuneiform language ('no proof of its correctness', p.143), not an observed stress system. Could alternatively be coded as stem-final (morphological) or weight-preferring penult; differs from the Akkadian weight rule in giving CVCCV̆Cum penult rather than initial stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Eblaite (ebla1238, ISO xeb), extinct East Semitic language of 3rd-millennium Ebla (Tell Mardikh, Syria). Peust's evidence comes specifically from manuscript B of the lexical list 'Vocabolario di Ebla' (nouns/infinitives with case endings); he notes other Eblaite text sources follow different l/r spelling conventions. The stress rule is a philological reconstruction, not an observed system.

sources.note: Sec. 3.5 'Stress' (p.234) states the weight-based rule for Akkadian only ('In Akkadian the stress of a given word is predictable...'); nothing is said about Eblaite stress; sec. 3.1.2 notes Eblaite phonology is knowable only within the limits of the syllabary. Silent on Eblaite stress.
